Half Plane Test

GeometryCoordinatesInduction
Game: Straight lines cut the board into sides, and the part shared by all of them is a convex shape; nothing is won or lost.
How to play: Drag a line to slide it, or drag the two dots at its ends to swing it. Use the buttons to change the number of lines, show the shared part, and press an arrow key after focusing a dot.

Drag the middle of a line to slide it. Drag a numbered dot to swing that line; with a dot focused, the arrow keys do the same.

Look for the math

Each line keeps one side of the board. Move the lines around and watch what is left where all the kept sides meet: the shape changes, but one thing about it never does.

One side of each line

A line splits the board into two half planes. Give the line a direction from its first dot to its second and calculate cross = (x2 − x1)(y − y1) − (y2 − y1)(x − x1). The applet keeps the side with cross > 0 — exactly what its FindOrientation bytecode tests. Drag a dot and the direction changes, so the kept side changes with it.

Why the overlap stays convex

Take any two points in the overlap. Each is inside every half plane, so the whole segment between them is inside every half plane too. That is the definition of a convex set. Add the lines one at a time: intersecting a convex set with one more convex half plane keeps it convex. That is the page's induction proof, and it works for any finite number of half planes. The logic test checked the midpoint property on thousands of pairs of points and found the overlap convex in all 400 configurations it tried.

A polygon, empty — or a strip

Inside the bounded drawing board, the overlap is always a convex polygon or nothing at all; the test found empty overlaps when two lines keep opposite outer strips. On the whole unbounded plane the page's wording needs a small caution: one half plane by itself goes on for ever, and two opposite ones can leave a strip or a single line. The board is what the applet draws, so on the board the claim holds as stated. The page's other claim about dragging was checked too: a pointer near an end swings the line around the opposite end, and a pointer in the middle slides it without turning it.

Small changes from the Java applet: a dragged dot follows the pointer instead of adding the raw mouse coordinates on every event, and a line is squeezed to the board while dragging rather than only when the mouse is released. The kept side, the 1 to 20 line range, the shaded overlap and the drag modes are unchanged.

Set 8 lines, tick Show overlap, then slide the highlighted line until the shaded polygon vanishes.
